Length Zero, Points Uncountable

This scene builds the Cantor set. Keep deleting middle thirds: the length dies to zero, yet uncountably many points survive.

Each deletion shrinks the total length to two-thirds. After infinitely many rounds, the length is zero. But some points are never cut away. There are as many of them as there are real numbers.

For example, cut the middle third out of a 🍰 cake. Then cut the middle of each remaining piece, again and again. The cake almost vanishes. Still, uncountably many spots were never touched by the knife.

Prove that the Cantor set CCC has measure zero, via a covering argument.

∀ ε>0  ∃ n: (23)n<ε\forall\, \varepsilon > 0\ \ \exists\, n:\ \left(\tfrac23\right)^n < \varepsilon∀ε>0  ∃n: (32​)n<ε
Show proof

  1. C⊆CnC \subseteq C_nC⊆Cn​ for every nnn, and CnC_nCn​ consists of 2n2^n2n intervals of total length (23)n\left(\frac23\right)^n(32​)n.

  2. Given ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0, choose nnn with (23)n<ε\left(\frac23\right)^n < \varepsilon(32​)n<ε (possible since (23)n→0\left(\frac23\right)^n \to 0(32​)n→0). Then CCC is covered by finitely many intervals of total length below ε\varepsilonε.

  3. A set coverable by intervals of arbitrarily small total length has measure zero (this is the definition of Lebesgue outer measure zero). For the record, CCC is also uncountable — length zero, yet uncountably many points.
